short: A component prepared in bulk and used across several dishes.
seoTitle: Sub-Recipe — Meaning and How to Cost One
metaDescription: A sub-recipe is a base gravy, stock or sauce made in bulk and used across several dishes. Costing it once and allocating it is where menu costing usually fails.
definition: A sub-recipe is a component prepared in bulk and used across several dishes — a base gravy, a stock, a spice mix, a sauce or a dough. It is costed once per batch and then charged into each finished dish at a per-unit rate.
bodyHtml:
Why sub-recipes break costing

Sub-recipes are where restaurant costing usually goes wrong. If a base gravy is treated as a lump kitchen expense rather than costed and allocated, every dish using it is understated — and the error is invisible, because each individual recipe costing sheet looks correct on its own.

How to cost a sub-recipe

Cost the batch at landed cost, divide by usable output rather than raw input, and carry that rate into each dish exactly the way you would carry a raw ingredient. Re-cost the sub-recipe whenever any of its inputs move, since one change ripples through every dish that uses it.

faq.question: How often should I re-cost a sub-recipe?
faq.answer: Whenever a major input price moves, and at least quarterly. One sub-recipe often feeds a third of the menu.

faq.question: Does a sub-recipe need its own yield?
faq.answer: Yes. Reduction, straining and trim all mean usable output is lower than raw input, and costing on raw input understates every dish.
